Bagpipes are very sensitive to temperature and moisture, the drones and the chanter reed will change surprisingly fast as conditions change. That includes setting it down in the sun, letting it get dry because you didn't play out for a couple days, or playing it for a long time in one sitting so that it picks up a lot of moisture. Like half of the time spent at band practice is tuning pipes so we're closer to each other.

Ways to correct the pitch of the chanter include adjusting the height that the reed sits at inside the chanter, narrowing or widening the air chamber inside the reed (squish with pliers), and putting strips of electrical tape over the tops of the finger holes. They used wax for that before they had tape, but this is a lot faster and more warm weather resistant.

Then there's the blowing pressure, lower pressure will make the chanter (melody notes) flatter, higher pressure will make it sharper, and that's assuming you're keeping it close enough not to cut out or start squawking. You can also hear if there's unsteady pressure in the drones, they can get flatter and maybe sort of growly if the pressure gets lower than they want.

Basically, I haven't been at it long enough or consistently enough to reliable tell whether stuff is sharp or flat, or whether it's in tune or merely close. I also need work on the skill of keeping the pressure steady between my breath and my arm, and just more strength and stamina for it.
